messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmad, a 40‑year‑old software engineer of Lebanese descent, had settled into a predictable rhythm in his coastal apartment and at his office in the tech park. On the morning of the 7.0 magnitude quake, he was in his kitchen, scrolling through code snippets, when the earth lurched and the building swayed. The ceiling cracked, glass shattered, and a metallic groan sounded like thunder. He remembered the shudder, the hiss of air through the broken pane, and the distant wail of sirens that soon would follow. The sudden violence of the event planted a seed of doubt in his mind: “If I had known the building’s foundations were weak, perhaps I could have escaped.” That self‑criticism blossomed into the trio of negative appraisals—self‑comparison, the belief that no good could happen, and the loss of his former happiness. These appraisals didn’t just linger; they sharpened his perception of danger. The thought that others had suffered less made him hyper‑aware of any sudden movement nearby, and the memory of the quake itself began to resurface whenever he heard the faint rumble of traffic, making him feel as if the world were still trembling. The vivid recollection—his ears flooded with the echo of sirens, his lungs filled with the smell of burnt plaster, his hands trembling—kept the memory of the disaster alive, blurring the order of what had happened. As the shock faded, he found himself forced to keep replaying the sequence: what had come first, what had followed, what had left him behind. That same vividness of recall carried him into the maladaptive strategies he now employed. When the memory surfaced, he would scramble to force his mind toward “at least I survived” to quell the panic, but that attempt at positive reframing was short‑lived. The urge to punish the unseen architects of his fate pulled him into a darker rumination about revenge, and the constant battle to silence those thoughts pushed him to avoid any medical cue—no visits to the clinic, no physical exams, no ambulance rides, even when his blood pressure spiked during an unrelated headache. Each time a memory resurfaced, his sense of threat sharpened: the sudden jolt of a door opening, the feel of a colleague’s hand brushing his arm while moving past him, the echo of a distant siren—all ignited the same fear that the world was still in motion, still threatening him. The more he clung to those thoughts, the more his negative appraisals deepened. The feeling that “no good ahead” seemed increasingly inevitable, and he began to feel his former happiness slipping further away. In the workplace, the threat signals were everyday. A passing coworker’s elbow could startle him, and the sudden creak of a hallway rail would set his heart racing. Even routine motions, like a colleague’s hand reaching for a file, became a trigger for alarm. The fear that anything could happen made Ahmad instinctively trace exit routes before he left the office, and he avoided the hospital when a colleague suggested a routine check‑up after a minor injury. Each startle response not only intensified his perception of danger but also pulled him back into the loop of recalling the quake. The thought of being surrounded by movement—whether a co‑worker’s brief hug or a sudden door slam—reminded him of the trembling building. The cycle fed on itself: the threat of movement heightened his maladaptive strategy of avoidance, which in turn reinforced the memory of that night and deepened his negative appraisals. Ahmad’s attempts to maintain a veneer of positivity—forcing himself to think “I am lucky” or “I survived”—became another reinforcement of his fear. When the threat of a routine office movement or a stranger’s touch triggered an alarm, he would retreat into his mental fortress, ruminate about revenge, and then retreat further from any physical examination. Each avoidance not only kept his negative appraisals in place—he believed that nothing good would come his way—but it also amplified his sense of threat. The loop tightened as he avoided hospitals, continued to re‑experience the quake with all five senses, and allowed his self‑critical appraisal to dictate his behavior at work and home. The feeling of lost happiness settled like a constant background hum, while the constant threat of an unexpected movement kept him in a state of perpetual readiness. When he finally decided to seek help, it was after a night in which his wife, Maya, pleaded with him not to stay up until dawn to “watch the news for any emergency alerts” because she feared he would be driven to the edge. The fear that he might again be swept away by a sudden quake—real or imagined—combined with the exhausting cycle of avoidance, pushed him toward a therapist. He is now most afraid that the loop will never break, that the quake will always be a shadow on his days, and he hopes to find a way to quiet the relentless startle, to let the memory fade without feeding the negative appraisals that keep him trapped in the present.
